Rev 00

Snap Circuits

Around age 7

My first electronics kit came with a manual of circuits to build. I worked through all of them quickly, and when the manual ran out, I started designing my own circuits with the same parts.

Reusing parts to build something new became a habit. About 30% of my 2026 ZVS driver (Rev 03) is built from salvaged components.

Rev 01

Mamut

May 2019

A solo line-following robot for the Intercolegiado de Robótica, held at the Gimnasio Campestre in Bogotá. My robotics tutor introduced me to Arduino. I built the robot and wrote its code, and he double-checked my work.

Mamut, named for its mammoth shell, was built from scratch rather than from a commercial line-following kit.

Second place
Rev 02

The fusor attempt

May–Jun 2024

The goal was a Farnsworth fusor: a device that confines plasma in a vacuum using a high-voltage electric field. It needs two halves, a high-voltage supply and a vacuum chamber. My school lent me its bell jar and vacuum pump, so I focused on the supply: a ZVS driver feeding a CRT flyback transformer.

I drew the schematic by hand and built it on a breadboard. It never produced high voltage.

Did not work
DC supply
ZVS driveroscillator
Flybackstep-up
Vacuum chambernever reached

What went wrong

  • Breadboard under load. A ZVS driver draws several amps; breadboard contacts and clip leads aren't rated for that.
  • Wrong resonant capacitor. The tank capacitor didn't match the circuit.
  • Wrong inductors. The inductors weren't suited to the current they had to carry.
  • It failed loudly. After weeks of burning smells and small pops, the circuit exploded. I pulled the plug in time, but left with a burn on my fingers and a permanent mark on my desk.
Rev 03

The ZVS driver

March 2026

Two years later, I tried again. I solved the parts problem from 2024 by shipping components to a family friend in Jacksonville and flying them home. About 30% of the build is salvaged (some capacitors, the inductors and the 10 kΩ resistors); the rest is new.

This time everything is soldered on perfboard, with the MOSFETs on heatsinks.

Working

Debug log

About 6 hours of soldering over March 5–6. The first power-on did nothing.

  1. Symptom

    Powered on at 17 V: no high-frequency hiss, no arc.

  2. Ruled out

    Swapped components one at a time to check for parts I'd damaged while soldering. No change.

  3. Isolate

    Disconnected one side of the primary winding (between a MOSFET drain and the center tap). A small arc appeared, so the flyback and secondary worked. The fault was in getting the oscillator to start.

  4. Root cause

    The power supply. A bench supply ramps its voltage up gradually, and a ZVS driver needs a fast-rising supply to start oscillating cleanly.

  5. Fix

    Re-soldered the primary and changed the startup sequence: connect the negative lead, switch the supply on at 17 V, then connect the positive lead. The circuit now sees full voltage at once. Result: the hiss, the smell of ozone, and a sustained arc.

Output estimate

≤ 50–60 kV

V ≈ d × Eb
Eb ≈ 30 kV/cm × 0.74 ≈ 22 kV/cm

d is the initial strike gap between the electrodes. The 0.74 factor corrects air's breakdown strength for Bogotá's altitude (about 2,600 m), where air is about 74% as dense as at sea level.

This is an upper bound: the uniform-field value overstates the voltage for pointed electrodes, which concentrate the field and break down at a lower average field.

Limits

  • Overdriven transformer. I drove the flyback past its rating for more output, knowing the trade-off. It failed a few months later.
  • Manual startup. The fix depends on connecting a lead by hand. A switch on the supply line would make the fast start repeatable.
